Question: What are the ways that differentiate a contract from a mere agreement and why does the law make the distinction between them?
Answer: I’m a bit confused by the question, so let’s make sure we’re speaking the same language. When you say “agreement” versus “contract,” are you meaning one document that can be legally enforceable versus another document that cannot be legally enforced? If that’s what you mean, then a “legally enforceable” contract generally requires a “bargained for exchange of value”. There are many exceptions, however, to what would be otherwise considered a legally enforceable contract, including (but not limited to) one party lacks capacity (i.e. a minor or protected adult), duress/coercion, against public policy, no specific term, etc. There are also exceptions where something could be legally enforceable, even though you do not have all the elements required to comprise a contract (i.e. offer, acceptance, consideration, etc). One exception would be “detrimental reliance.” Not all the states have the same definition for this, but in general, if one party “detrimentally relied” on the statements or actions or inactions of another party, to his or her detriment, there are circumstances when this could be enforceable.

Question: Can a Canadian Ontario Corp run payroll (issue W2s & 1099) for its US residents employees. If so what does it need in US to do that? EIN#? Bank account? Address (physical or virtual?). Or does it need to have a Corp (Delaware or any other) to do so?
Answer: This is a great question. The quick answer is “yes,” a Canadian company can hire US-based resident employees. The question is “how.” (What I’m about to say applies to W2-based employees, not 1099-based employees.) The Canadian company (or any company located outside the US) must first “domesticate” in the United States. It does this by filing a foreign entity filing in the state (or states) it is doing business. Typically, this means where you have W2-based employees, at a minimum. If you’re “generally selling stuff on the Internet,” and selling to all 50 states, that does not mean you need to file in all 50 states. But, if you have a W2 employee in NY and IL, then it means those two states. If you’re selling services or products primarily to a large customer in PA, then it means that state, too. My law firm offers low-cost, flat-rate fees for foreign filings, but it does depend on what type of entity you have. You did say “Corp” above, so here’s our link for foreign corporations: Foreign Corporation Registration | Law 4 Small Business, P.C. (L4SB). Once you have at least one foreign filing in the US, you will need to get a FEIN. In order to do that, you will need to indicate a “Responsible Party” to the IRS who either controls or owns (even partially) the company. That Responsible Party must have a FEIN (for another company), a SSN (for a US-based citizen) or a ITIN (for anyone issued an “International Taxpayer Identification Number). With the FEIN, you can then do withholding and more. It is NOT necessary to have a US-based bank account. Depending on the state where you foreign file, you may or may not need a US-based address. The general rule is: It can be located anywhere, but it cannot be a PO Box. There are at least three states that don’t follow this general rule: AZ, OR and CA. For AZ and CA, you can use a “virtual address” located in the state. For OR, the legislature there are complete fools, and they won’t even permit a virtual address. In order for you to comply with their “doing business in the state” laws, they require you to actually rent or lease space on behalf of the company. I’m hoping some one will sue the State of Oregon, because they are being absolutely ridiculous. You do NOT need to form an actual corporation in the US. The foreign filing is sufficient. Larry.

Question: Is a contract valid if it releases a party from liability for probable injury?
Answer: If we assume all other aspects of the contract are valid and acceptable, such as “consideration,” then such a contract would not be invalid simply because it releases a party from liability for probable injury (sorry for the use of a double-negative here). Contract law is a very complex area of law, and believe it or not, there is a distinction between a contract being valid but unenforceable versus invalid on its face (i.e. voidable versus void contracts). I would argue simply releasing a party from liability for probably injury does not make a contract void simply because of the fact that it releases a party from liability for probable injury. You COULD have a VOIDABLE contract, if there were other deficiencies in the contract, but such deficiencies aren’t dependent or related to the issue of releasing a party from liability for probably injury. Such deficiencies could include: lack of consideration, undue influence, coercion or threats, party lacks capacity, etc. This is a good question, and is why we recommend business leaders never sign contracts without getting a lawyer involved. The legal issues can be very complicated and the results surprising. We have a low-cost, flat-rate fee of $20/page to review contracts if you’re interested. Learn more here: Landing Page: Flat-Rate Contract Review | Law 4 Small Business, P.C. (L4SB). Thank you. Larry.

Question: What is a bill of sale and how is it legally binding?
Answer: When we use a “Bill of Sale” in a transaction, it is usually accompanied by a “Purchase Agreement” of some type, among other potential documents, including promissory note, corporate formation documents (i.e. revised ByLaws or Operating Agreement), etc. A Bill of Sale is a legal document, but I hesitate to actually call it a “contract” for the purchase of personal property (as opposed to real estate). The reason is, a Bill of Sale is usually a very simple document that outlines the purchase price, and sometimes (not always) enumerates “what is purchased.” The “what is purchased” part is usually a high-level list of what is purchased (such as in a business transaction) that separates into IRS taxable categories. What you won’t find in a Bill of Sale, are the general terms of the sale, such as conditions precedent (i.e. what has to be in place before the sale takes place), representations and warranties (i.e. that the seller has good title, hasn’t encumbered the property being sold, condition of assets, etc), payment terms, closing date, etc, etc, etc. I tell my clients to think of the “Bill of Sale” as a “receipt” more than the contract regulating the transaction or purchase. Given it’s simplicity, there really isn’t much to enforce. If it’s the only document in the transaction, you better hope it has enough specificity to fully identify the transaction to make it enforceable. If it doesn’t have enough information, we need to fall back to other aspects of contract law, including but not limited to the Parol Evidence Rule, Detrimental Reliance, etc, to determine whether we can introduce additional evidence to make a legal argument to enforce a Bill of Sale, especially if there was some form of detrimental reliance on behalf of the buyer (i.e. paying money) or seller. Larry.

Being registered in the State is a sufficient nexus. Second rule: you want to use a state as your “choice of law” forum that you think favors the legal situation or situations important to your business. What does this mean between WY and NM? Well, for example, NM’s laws in consumer protection are fairly basic. WY’s laws are a bit more progressive and modern. As another example, I believe the State of NM just updated its regulations to put “e-cigs” at the same level as tobacco-based cigarets, while that hasn’t happened yet in WY (I’m not a WY attorney, so please double-check this if you’re in the e-cig business). Depending on your industry and business, picking one state over the other could have profound impacts on how your contracts are interpreted and how much liability your company could have in certain causes of action, claims, judgements and lawsuits. Those are the biggies, but there are others. Our firm is very good at setting up Anonymous LLC’s and answering questions. To learn more, go to Maintain Your Privacy With an Anonymous LLC | Law 4 Small Business, P.C. (L4SB). Thank you. Larry.

Name: Larry Donahue
Question: Where should I file an LLC if my friend that lives in Idaho and I who lives in New Jersey, are starting a Social Media marketing Agency, when the business will be online and we could have customers in multiple states? What should we do?
Answer: My recommendation is to ask yourself these questions, and follow this general framework: (1) Will you be (eventually) paying yourselves W2 income? If so, you’re doing business in BOTH states, and trying to figure out which state is less expensive is irrelevant. You file in either state as your primary state, and the other state as a Foreign LLC. (2) Do you care about anonymity? If so, then (for all states except CA) you’re going to need a child LLC as your Operating Company in either one of your states of residence, which will be owned by an Anonymous LLC as a holding company parent (learn more here: Preserving Anonymity in a State that Discloses Ownership Information). You file the operating child LLC as a Foreign LLC in the other state. (3) Assuming you’re following the framework above, then you may need to register in other states you’re conducting business. This is a hard analysis, since each state has its own rules around this. But, if any of the below is true, then you should register (as a Foreign LLC, in each state you’re conducting business) your LLC (if #1 above applies) or your operating child LLC (if #2 applies). Good luck to you. Larry.

Question: What are my options if a researcher has knowledge I want, but is prevented from giving it to me by contract (with two unrelated companies)?
Answer: The short answer is you’re “SOL,” for “s**t out of luck.” The longer answer is: Can you and the scientist figure out a permissible reason to share the information with you? To answer that question, you need to examine the contracts the scientist has with the other two companies. Sometimes, they may allow sharing of information if the newcomer simply signs a NDA. I’ve seen other contracts where confidential information may be shared in certain circumstances. Is the information the scientist’s intellectual property or confidential information or the other companies? If the scientist’s, then perhaps you wait out the contracts? If the other companies, which seems a bit strange — how would the scientist come into possession of the same confidential information from two different companies — unless it’s not the same confidential information you seek, or there’s some relationship between the two, then you may not have any options. It all depends how those contracts read. Good luck to you. Larry.

Question: I want to start my own video production company. I have a website and I get clients, do I have to register my company?
Answer: Do you **have to register your company?** The quick answer is “no,” as all states permit individuals to operate as a “sole proprietorship” (assuming you’re the only owner). However, did you know that video production is actually a risky business? Why? Because you have a lot of potential liability that can attach to the company, and therefore you personally — if you’re operating as a sole proprietorship versus a properly formed company. The biggest liability comes from third-party liability associated with copyright infringement or invasion of privacy. The copyright problem comes from several angles. First, a client asks you to include specific photos, music or video in a production. If the client doesn’t have a right to this material, you can be liable to the third-party (even if it’s material provided to you by the client). Second, if you’re doing a photo shoot and capture some background music or wall pictures, you could be subject to copyright infringement of those copyrighted objects. Third, I’ve seen clients come back and sue the production company, because the clients said they were expecting the production company to deal with the licensing or otherwise “produce around” copyrighted objects. The invasion of privacy issue comes around, simply because you’re included the likeness of a third-party without their permission. No proper release or permissions. This can even happen from — again — client supplied material. What are the chances you can have a problem with the above? No clue. Depends on the nature of your business, your clients and your level of luck. If you do have a problem or complaint against you, I can tell you that it will cost thousands of dollars to defend yourself, usually with a claim of at least $10,000 or MUCH MORE. You will wish you had a company that you could potentially walk away from versus having to fork out thousands with no sure chance of winning. My advice for the reasons above, is not to roll the dice. The price is very cost-effective for the liability protection that is provided. You can learn more, see pricing and order using the following link from my company, if you’re interested: Form a Limited Liability Company (LLC) | Law 4 Small Business, P.C. (L4SB). Thank you. Larry.

Question: What is a holding company LLC?
Answer: A “Holding Company LLC” is: Holding companies that are limited liability companies (LLC’s) are important because they are not operating a business. They are holding something. As such, they generally do NOT NEED to register anywhere, which helps in two important areas: You can control where profits and losses from subsidiaries (or companies owned by the holding company) go, which is a form of tax management. You can also control what “ownership information” is publicly displayed for the assets being held by a holding company, thereby helping to maintain a level of anonymity if you’re careful about it. Larry.

Question: As an owner of a business what are the legal ramifications of running family member loans through the business?
Answer: I don’t exactly know what you mean by “running … loans through the business.” Do you mean… If you mean #1, I don’t think it’s a problem at all, although I would advise that you have a standard promissory note between the business and the family member, with a fair-market-rate of interest charged. There can be tax consequences to one or both parties if you don’t do this right. If you mean #2, that would be a very, very bad idea. Question: What are some important clauses to include in a distributions agreement?
Answer: I think Mr. Kumar Verma provided a very comprehensive answer, although I will say that there’s quite a bit of beef that is still missing. Under “confidentiality,” you may want to include a clause about Trade Secrets. Under “Termination,” you really want to get specific about what factors could lead to termination for cause, as well as you may want to consider a “liquidated damages” clause for certain types of breaches. Name: Larry Donahue
Question: So, I understand that you can use a post office or mailing building address for your LLC (when filing for the EIN or registered Agent). Would you have to ask such places if you want to use their address for your own LLC?
Answer: Some great answers are here already, so I won’t repeat them except to say the following: (1) Can you use someone’s address, not your own that you don’t control, such as your Registered Agent’s (RA) address, without their permission? The answer is “no.” This would (a) violate USPS regulations; (b) permit whomever’s address to simply not deliver your mail to you; (c) permit them to report you to the USPS; and (d) most importantly, this could be considered a “fraudulent filing”, allowing a clever plaintiff’s attorney to argue to “pierce the corporate veil” thereby destroying any liability protection you were hoping to achieve with your LLC. (2) If the RA gives you permission to use their address, then can you use it? The answer is still “no,” because see (1)(a) and (1)(d) above. This violates USPS regulations, because any third-party mail receiving agency must abide by the USPS CMRA regulations, and that requires filing out Form 1583. We do a LOT of regular LLC filings and anonymous LLC’s, and we won’t let folks use our RA address for their business address because of (1)(a) and (1)(d) above. It does put us at a competitive disadvantage when so much of our competition does this, but as attorneys, we aren’t paid just to create a LLC, but to make sure it’s done right. Larry.

Question: What is the best corporate structure for a digital marketing startup, an LLC or an S Corp?
Answer: Just to be clear, your best two options are: Each can be taxed as (depending on number of owners, and other limitations): LLC’s can also be taxed as disregarded and partnership, depending on number of owners. Therefore, your question isn’t “LLC versus S-Corp.” It’s actually “LLC versus Corporation,” and then you can tax either under Subchapter S (i.e. S-Corp). Unfortunately, Trump’s tax reform act of 2017 complicates matters. Prior to this act, the LLC and Corporation (when taxed under Subchapter S) were virtually identical from a tax perspective. Trump’s tax reform act does favor a Corporation in certain narrow circumstances that I don’t fully understand, because I’m not a tax attorney. We did put an AI-based “entity selection tool” together, that factors all sorts of things, including anonymity, taxes, citizenship, state location and more. It only takes a few minutes, if you’re interested. You can find it here: Business Entity Selector Tool | Law 4 Small Business, P.C. (L4SB). In most circumstances, LLC’s are favored simply because they tend to be less expensive to own and operate, and they less burdens associated with reporting and closing down. Corporations are more formal structures, which come with additional costs in establishing, maintaining, annual reporting and shutting down. But, if you can have some tax savings, it may make sense to go with a Corporation. The rules are complicated, and so far none of the answers I’ve seen for this question remotely deal with these issues. Our entity selection tool does. Take it for a spin. Good luck to you. Larry.

Question: If an LLC member engages in behavior that jeopardizes the business, how do other members pursue an involuntary withdraw (IW) of that member? The OA specifies that a member is subject to IW if doing that behavior.
Answer: The quick answer is that the other Members hold a meeting and vote the infringing Member out of the LLC, and then issue a notice of the same to such Member. The better answer, however, is you should hire a business attorney IN THE STATE YOUR LLC WAS FORMED, to help make sure you do this correctly. You want to make sure you have the right evidence and proof, so if sued you can easily defend yourself. Also, rarely are things so clean — you not only need to follow the OA to the letter, but you need to reference statute in areas where there are gaps in the OA. For example, how do you deal with any capital accounts as well as the value associated with the dissociating Member’s ownership? Good luck to you. Larry.

Question: What does LLC mean?
Answer: “LLC” is an abbreviation for “limited liability company.” A limited liability company, or LLC, is a type of corporate entity that is favored by smaller and medium-sized organizations because of its low-cost, simplicity and ease of maintenance over time. LLC should be contrasted with a “corporation,” which is also another form of corporate entity. Corporations are generally considered “more formal” corporate structures, and therefore a bit more costly and a bit more difficult to setup and maintain. There are vast differences between the two types of corporate entities or structures, and you should consult with a business attorney to determine which is best for you. The answer generally varies on whether you intend to go public some day, what state you would form in, your tax preferences and more. For more information, you may be interested in our two links. For LLC’s, go here: Form a Limited Liability Company (LLC) | Law 4 Small Business, P.C. (L4SB). For Corporations, go here: Form a Corporation | Law 4 Small Business, P.C. (L4SB). Thank you. Larry.
